json.out/captions.srt:
1
00:00:00,000 --> 00:00:03,477
Type a word into a dictionary app and the
definition is just there.

2
00:00:03,797 --> 00:00:05,696
Not "searching," not a spinner.

3
00:00:06,016 --> 00:00:06,849
There.

4
00:00:06,987 --> 00:00:10,077
And that word could have been any of a few
hundred thousand others.

5
00:00:10,144 --> 00:00:13,963
Somewhere underneath, a program found the
one entry you wanted without looking at

6
00:00:14,030 --> 00:00:15,030
the ones you didn't.

7
00:00:15,264 --> 00:00:17,227
Not by being fast at checking.

8
00:00:17,547 --> 00:00:19,147
By not checking at all.

9
00:00:19,467 --> 00:00:20,853
That's a hash table.

10
00:00:21,173 --> 00:00:24,873
By the end of this you'll know exactly how
a piece of text turns into a place to

11
00:00:24,940 --> 00:00:29,093
look, and why that trick can also go wrong
in a way that's bitten real production

12
00:00:29,160 --> 00:00:29,993
systems.

13
00:00:34,101 --> 00:00:35,829
Say what you'd try first.

14
00:00:36,149 --> 00:00:39,989
Keep the entries in a list and check them
one at a time until one matches.

15
00:00:40,309 --> 00:00:41,226
That works.

16
00:00:41,546 --> 00:00:45,898
It's also the whole problem: to find one
item you may have to look at all of them.

17
00:00:46,218 --> 00:00:48,842
Twice as many entries, twice as long a
wait.

18
00:00:49,162 --> 00:00:53,831
That's linear time, and it does not scale
to the millions of rows a real database or

19
00:00:53,898 --> 00:00:57,056
the tens of thousands of variables a real
compiler is tracking.

20
00:00:57,376 --> 00:01:01,121
You can do better by keeping the list
sorted and halving the search space each

21
00:01:01,188 --> 00:01:03,588
step, the way you'd find a name in a phone
book.

22
00:01:03,690 --> 00:01:07,531
That's logarithmic time, a real
improvement a million entries drops to

23
00:01:07,598 --> 00:01:09,898
about twenty comparisons instead of a
million.

24
00:01:10,197 --> 00:01:14,331
But twenty comparisons is still not zero,
and it grows, just slowly, as the table

25
00:01:14,398 --> 00:01:15,231
grows.

26
00:01:15,402 --> 00:01:19,301
And keeping the list sorted costs you
every time you insert something new shift

27
00:01:19,368 --> 00:01:21,482
everything over to make room, or re-sort.

28
00:01:21,802 --> 00:01:24,597
None of that goes away, it just gets
cheaper per step.

29
00:01:24,917 --> 00:01:28,202
What you actually want is to skip the
comparisons entirely.

30
00:01:28,522 --> 00:01:29,952
Not search faster.

31
00:01:30,272 --> 00:01:31,722
Not search at all.

32
00:01:39,177 --> 00:01:41,225
Here's the idea that gets you there.

33
00:01:41,545 --> 00:01:45,236
Instead of asking "where in this list is
my item," compute where it is.

34
00:01:45,556 --> 00:01:48,806
Take the key the word, the username,
whatever you're looking up and run it

35
00:01:48,872 --> 00:01:51,164
through a function that turns it into a
number.

36
00:01:51,230 --> 00:01:54,260
Not a meaningful number, not an ID anyone
assigned it.

37
00:01:54,580 --> 00:01:59,286
Just an arithmetic mess of the key's bits,
chosen so that similar keys land on wildly

38
00:01:59,352 --> 00:02:00,297
different outputs.

39
00:02:00,617 --> 00:02:04,596
That's a hash function, and the number it
produces, reduced to fit your array size,

40
00:02:04,662 --> 00:02:05,495
is an index.

41
00:02:05,737 --> 00:02:07,636
Store the value at that index.

42
00:02:07,956 --> 00:02:11,186
To look it up again, don't search hash the
key a second time, get the same number

43
00:02:11,252 --> 00:02:12,734
back, and go straight there.

44
00:02:13,054 --> 00:02:15,657
One computation, one array access, done.

45
00:02:15,977 --> 00:02:17,662
That's the whole mechanism.

46
00:02:17,982 --> 00:02:20,628
Average case, that's constant time: O(1).

47
00:02:20,948 --> 00:02:24,756
The size of the table barely matters,
because you never touch the entries you're

48
00:02:24,822 --> 00:02:25,662
not looking for.

49
00:02:25,982 --> 00:02:30,916
The entire cost of a hash table lives in
one guarantee: the same key always hashes

50
00:02:30,982 --> 00:02:32,041
to the same number.

51
00:02:32,361 --> 00:02:34,324
Break that, and nothing else works.

52
00:02:41,545 --> 00:02:44,595
Walk through it with three words and an
array of eight slots.

53
00:02:44,894 --> 00:02:47,284
Hash "cat," and say it comes out to 2.

54
00:02:47,604 --> 00:02:49,481
Slot 2 now holds cat.

55
00:02:49,801 --> 00:02:52,020
Hash "dog," it comes out to 5.

56
00:02:52,340 --> 00:02:54,153
Slot 5 holds dog.

57
00:02:54,473 --> 00:02:56,820
Two lookups, two slots, no scanning.

58
00:02:57,140 --> 00:02:58,462
Now hash "owl.

59
00:02:58,782 --> 00:03:02,089
Same function, same rules and it also
comes out to 2.

60
00:03:02,409 --> 00:03:04,329
Two different keys, one slot.

61
00:03:04,649 --> 00:03:08,017
That's a collision, and with only eight
slots and an unbounded number of possible

62
00:03:08,084 --> 00:03:10,836
words, it is not a bug, it is a certainty.

63
00:03:11,156 --> 00:03:14,057
This is where the "average case" in O(1)
is hiding.

64
00:03:14,377 --> 00:03:18,437
The fix used here is chaining: slot 2
doesn't hold one value, it holds a tiny

65
00:03:18,504 --> 00:03:19,302
list.

66
00:03:19,369 --> 00:03:20,841
Cat is still first.

67
00:03:21,161 --> 00:03:24,126
Owl gets appended right after it in that
same slot.

68
00:03:24,446 --> 00:03:28,487
Looking up owl now costs two comparisons
instead of one still nowhere near scanning

69
00:03:28,554 --> 00:03:30,740
the whole table, but not free either.

70
00:03:31,060 --> 00:03:33,662
That's the trade the whole structure is
built on.

71
00:03:33,982 --> 00:03:37,837
A good hash function spreads keys thinly
enough that most slots hold zero or one

72
00:03:37,904 --> 00:03:40,510
entries and collisions stay rare and
short.

73
00:03:40,830 --> 00:03:44,777
A bad one piles everything into a handful
of slots and you've quietly rebuilt the

74
00:03:44,844 --> 00:03:48,169
linear scan you were trying to escape, one
chain at a time.

75
00:03:48,489 --> 00:03:50,708
Chaining isn't the only fix, either.

76
00:03:51,028 --> 00:03:54,617
Open addressing skips the linked list and,
on a collision, just probes forward to the

77
00:03:54,684 --> 00:03:59,637
next empty slot in the array itself slot
3, then 4, then 5 and remembers to keep

78
00:03:59,704 --> 00:04:01,097
probing on lookup too.

79
00:04:01,417 --> 00:04:05,747
No extra memory for pointers, but the
table fills up faster and probing gets

80
00:04:05,814 --> 00:04:06,900
longer as it does.

81
00:04:07,220 --> 00:04:09,801
Different trade, same underlying problem.

82
00:04:19,432 --> 00:04:22,975
This isn't a theory exercise it's the data
structure under Python's dict,

83
00:04:23,042 --> 00:04:26,792
JavaScript's object and Map, and every
language's HashMap.

84
00:04:27,112 --> 00:04:31,118
Every one of them is quietly running this
same array-plus-hash-function design under

85
00:04:31,185 --> 00:04:32,552
a much friendlier name.

86
00:04:32,872 --> 00:04:35,069
Two things keep it fast in practice.

87
00:04:35,389 --> 00:04:38,675
First, load factor: the fraction of slots
that are occupied.

88
00:04:38,995 --> 00:04:42,648
Push that too high and collisions stop
being rare chains get long and you're back

89
00:04:42,715 --> 00:04:43,548
to scanning.

90
00:04:43,688 --> 00:04:47,208
So implementations track it, and once it
crosses a threshold, usually around

91
00:04:47,275 --> 00:04:51,838
seventy percent, they allocate a bigger
array, often double the size, and re-hash

92
00:04:51,905 --> 00:04:53,800
every existing key into a new slot.

93
00:04:54,120 --> 00:04:57,968
Expensive when it happens, but it happens
rarely enough that the average cost per

94
00:04:58,035 --> 00:04:59,389
insert stays constant.

95
00:04:59,709 --> 00:05:03,928
Second, and this one is easy to miss: the
hash function itself has to be hard to

96
00:05:03,995 --> 00:05:04,845
reverse-engineer.

97
00:05:05,128 --> 00:05:08,148
If an attacker can predict which keys
collide, they can hand your server

98
00:05:08,215 --> 00:05:12,193
thousands of keys that all pile into one
slot on purpose, turning every one of your

99
00:05:12,260 --> 00:05:15,091
O(1) lookups into an O(n) scan at once.

100
00:05:15,411 --> 00:05:19,558
That's not hypothetical it's a real
denial-of-service class, and it's why

101
00:05:19,625 --> 00:05:23,538
production hash tables seed their hash
function with randomness that changes

102
00:05:23,605 --> 00:05:25,373
every time the program starts.

103
00:05:33,639 --> 00:05:35,090
Three things to keep.

104
00:05:35,410 --> 00:05:40,214
A hash function turns a key into an index,
so lookup becomes one computation instead

105
00:05:40,280 --> 00:05:41,113
of a search.

106
00:05:41,340 --> 00:05:45,214
Collisions aren't an edge case, they're
guaranteed once your key space is bigger

107
00:05:45,280 --> 00:05:49,534
than your table, so every real hash table
has a plan for them chaining is one, there

108
00:05:49,600 --> 00:05:50,433
are others.

109
00:05:50,663 --> 00:05:54,804
And load factor is the number that decides
when the table has to grow, trading an

110
00:05:54,870 --> 00:05:57,490
expensive rehash now for cheap lookups
after.

111
00:05:57,810 --> 00:06:01,644
That word "hash function" is doing more
work than we gave it credit for here I

112
00:06:01,710 --> 00:06:04,764
treated it like a black box that just
spreads keys around.

113
00:06:05,084 --> 00:06:09,154
Make that box impossible to run backwards,
and you don't just get a fast lookup

114
00:06:09,220 --> 00:06:09,968
table.

115
00:06:10,034 --> 00:06:14,172
You get the one-way function underneath
password storage and digital signatures.

116
00:06:14,492 --> 00:06:15,474
That's next.
